utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I give the floor to Mr. Scott to use up the two hours that remain for him, the registrar forwarded Mr. Karnavas's request to us that concerns preliminary questions put to the witness as an expert witness. We have already orally rejected this request. The Chamber, Mr. Karnavas, is somewhat surprised given that, in spite of our oral rejection of this request, written submissions were provided to the registry. Is there any explanation for this, since you gave this request to registry and we dealt with this request orally last time it was mentioned? The one that was forwarded to the registry is dated the 4th of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat what I said. Mr. Karnavas, before the beginning of the examination of the witness, you took the floor and you told us that before the examination you wanted the Chamber to grant you leave to put a series of written questions to the person in question. There were 60 questions in total. The Judges decided otherwise. We decided that it was -- there was no reason to follow such procedure. And I did tell you that in the case of the cross-examination, you had the possibility of putting these 60 questions to the witness. But this morning we have discovered that you provided the registry with this document which was filed as a motion or a written submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can explain. It was -- that's the same submission that I filed in court, Your Honour, and as I understand it, these submissions also have to be filed electronically, so that may be the reason. But it's the same submission. It's nothing in addition to that. I apologise if it's caused any concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Scott, you have two hours at your disposal. If you take up less time, the Trial Chamber will be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, we ended yesterday talking about the HVO Herceg-Bosna, again, structures and processes dealing with the operation of various prisons and camps and we'd already gone through approximately five documents dealing with the establishment of the camps, some of them. Let me go forward with that same topic. After some of the situations and conditions and circumstances in these camps became more widely known, did your work -- did your report include a consideration of what HVO processes and structures were involved in dealing with the camps and prisons at that point?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I took a look at their -- the reaction of the HVO organs to these problems, much of which was discussed in the meetings of the HVO HZ HB, amongst other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I next ask you to look at Exhibit P 03673. As soon as you have that, can you tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement which was forwarded to all media, or released to all media, which is forwarding a message or a written response which Mr. Prlic gave to the Prime Minister of -- or the Deputy Prime Minister of Croatia, Mr. Mate Granic, on the 23rd of July, 1993, which is in response to a letter of Mr. Granic's which -- excuse me. That isn't. Yes, it is in response to Mr. Granic's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Are the two principal topics or subjects of this letter the circumstances concerning the detention camps and also the movement of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to direct your attention to the bottom part of the first page, starting with the words "The assault by Muslim forces ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The assault by Muslim forces on the region around Mostar compelled the armed forces of the HVO and its military police to assume preventive measures against all members of the so-called army of BiH and its active duty and reserve force in the area of combat activities. There were no special detention camps formed for these persons. Instead, the following facilities were used: Premises of the former military college, the nearby military base of the former JNA in Rodoc near Mostar (so-called 'Heliodrom'), as well as facilities once used for mass accommodation of JNA soldiers in Dretelj. It is necessary to keep in mind that these persons are all men in the age suitable for military service."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there. Going back to the earlier part of that paragraph on the previous page, were you familiar with the circumstances, situation, in early July, 1993, in which large numbers of Muslim men were arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does that appear to be what is being described here in terms of referring to the preventive measures against all members of the so-called army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what's being referred to here, the detention of Muslim males in the Heliodrom and other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me go back, then, further to the next -- again, back to the second page where you left off. Do you see the passage that starts "On the 22nd of June ..."?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you pick up at that point, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 22nd of June this year, more than 200 persons were released from the 'Heliodrom'. It is necessary to point out that all other persons (women, children and the elderly), who had been temporarily displaced outside of the town for the purpose of securing them from active combat activities (Article 49 of the Geneva Convention on the Protection of Civilians During War), were returned" and here illegible word, "addresses."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's stop there.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: End quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist the Judges in reference to the circumstances or the time when women, children, and elderly had been held for a time, when that had occurred approximately during this general period of time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would have been early -- I'm not -- actually, I'm not sure exactly of the time. I know that occurred in June, and I believe there were also detentions in early May of 1993 in Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we leave this document, to continue on schedule, can I ask you, although we're talking primarily about camps, since we have this document, if you look at the latter part of that document, on the bottom of that page and continuing on to the next page, does it also touch upon the issue of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It makes reference to the Makarska agreement, with is an agreement which had been reached not long before this regarding the free passage of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether that was a matter of some international attention as of midsummer of 1993, that is, getting humanitarian aid into the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and particularly into the eastern half of Mostar. It was very much a pressing issue for the international community active there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether any international pressure had been brought on the Republic of Croatia to gain access, humanitarian access to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head I can't recall if this was done at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let us go on, please, to Exhibit 35 -- P 03560. Can you tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are translations of minutes of the 46th session of the HVO HZ HB held on the 19th of July, 1993, and presided by Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, please, to page 4 under item 7 -- beginning at item 7.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to read out the passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an important passage. "After a discussion of the request by the HVO of Capljina municipality to relocate prisoners and a discussion of the status and accommodation conditions of prisoners and persons in isolation, with the aim of improving their accommodation conditions and overcoming the newly arisen situation, unanimous approval was given to adopt the following: "Conclusions. "1. Security accommodation conditions, material, and medical support for prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Convention relevant to the Treatment of Prisoners of War."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Relative."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said "relevant" and not "relative".

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moving on into the next paragraph: "If the existing accommodation conditions are not satisfactory, the head of the department of justice and general administration, in coordination with the Defence Department and the Department of the Interior shall designate new sites and transfer prisoners of war." Next paragraph: "The Defence Department shall be in charge of --," and there is a question as to whether this word is "their", "-- stay at the new sites."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then before putting some additional questions to you about this, on the following page, page 2, a working group to address these matters was formed, including among its members, as stated in this document, Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Working group to visit Capljina and inspect the conditions of the prisoners in Capljina included Berislav Pusic, Darinko Tadic, who was from the Office of the Displaced Persons and Refugees, and the department head, Zoran Buntic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward from the two documents we've looked at so far, can you give the Judges sort of an overview of what your research showed in terms of what happened then in the wake of these documents in connection with the HVO dealings and handling of matters concerning the camps as of the end of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these inspections were carried out. There was a meeting, I believe, soon afterwards regarding that and yet more bodies and institutions were created to deal with this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next ask you to look at Exhibit P 03565 --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- which you may have looked at previously for other circumstances, but we can look at it again, particularly paragraphs 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision of the HVO HZ HB from the same day as this meeting, from the 19th of July, with the name of Jadranko Prlic at the bottom and his signature, repeating the same decision to form the working group, and the other conclusions which were met in this meeting are reissued here as a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can I direct your attention to paragraph 7 of that document, and can you give the Judges any assistance as to why it was that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia needs to be informed concerning the entire problem?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two reasons. One, at this point already Mate Granic had taken an interest in these problems, as we saw from the earlier exhibit, and also because the international community had been putting pressure on the Republic of Croatia over these issues, and it was their problem as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this time period, did people involved with running these prisons continue to make reports about conditions and circumstances that existed at these camps and prisons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few. And for the purposes of my report, I've only cited a few of those reports, and those reports which go to the top level of the HVO -- top levels of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As one example, can I ask you to please go to Exhibit P 04352. And as soon as you have that, sir, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter from the director or warden of the Heliodrom camp, Mr. Stanko Bozic, to Mr. Bruno Stojic on the 20th of August, 1993, and he's informing him of the results of a visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross to that particular detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the last sentence in the second paragraph, will you read that sentence and the three bullet points, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Mr. Franko pointed to the following wrongdoings in violation of the Geneva Conventions: "1. Sending detainees to work. "2. The quality and quantity of foods (they request its improvement); and "3. Bad conditions in solitary cells."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Next paragraph: "Regarding the violations of the Geneva Conventions, Mr. Franko warned and obligated me as the warden to make sure that these wrongdoings are not repeated in the future or we would be reported to the International Tribunal. After the Red Cross's departure, we were not able to remedy these wrongdoings. On the contrary, the number of wounded and killed at the workplace is increasing by the day."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Period, closed quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did there continue, then, to be an exchange of information and correspondence among the senior HVO leadership and bodies concerning these issues?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was discussed quite a great deal after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention next to Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Can you tell us, Mr. Tomljanovich, who decided on the fact that prisoners were taken to work? Was this the governor's decision or, as one must assume, reading him, someone else's over whom he had no control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That appears to be the case. I didn't go into that sort of detail in the report, and I haven't reviewed any of those records for this report, but I know from what I've seen in the past that quite frequently prisoners were taken out of camps for work at the front lines in opposition to the wishes of the camp director. And there's a great deal of documentation on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very rapid question that I'd like to put to you. I don't want to interrupt the Prosecution, but it seems important to me. The document you examined has a certain number on it, and this document is a document that follows on the -- after other documents. Have you been able to examine all the documents from this prison? It's a document that follows on another form of correspondence. Is this the only document you saw, or were you able to examine other documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that this is not the only document from Mr. Bozic from that year. Whether or not we possess a complete set of his correspondence for that year I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question: After this letter that was addressed to Mr. Stojic was forwarded, was there a response? Did you find a reply from Mr. Stojic, a response to this letter, which is in fact a letter that calls for a reply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, which doesn't mean that one did not exist. But I did not see one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have another question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the same letter we can see that it says that the number of wounded and killed at their place of work increased from day to day when you were involved in your investigations. Did you find out whether they were wounded at work, or was this something that was inflicted on them? Were they wounded as a result of an accident, or were they maltreated? How is it that they were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure which particular incidents happened in which camp in which particular period of time, although I know that both incidents occurred rather frequently; that prisoners were wounded and killed both while being taken out to work and there were incidents in the camps as well. But as to what would have been going on in the Heliodrom at that particular time, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might just represent to the Court, the Court, of course, will be hearing a number of witnesses, including victims, people who were held in the camps who were taken out on work details and will tell in much more detail about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then next go, please, to Exhibit P 03663. And as soon as you have that, sir, will you tell us what that is and how, again, it relates to the current topic in your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are decisions adopted at a meeting of the -- in the military police administration of the HVO in Ljubuski on the 22nd of July, 1993, and the minutes are written up the next day, and signed by officer Zvonko Vidovic regarding this meeting at which the placing of prisoners in camps was addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does it indicate in the first paragraph any senior officials who were involved in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This meeting included, aside from the chief of the administration, Mr. Coric, all the chiefs of all the departments of the military police administration were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can I direct your attention, please, to the third paragraph starting with the word "Consequently." Would you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Consequently, all those persons who have been detained but against whom criminal proceedings have not been initiated (or against whom a criminal report has not been filed) are, according to the chief of the military police administration, unknown to our department. This refers solely to the large number of Muslims who have been brought unselectively to the SVIZ," in brackets the extension of that acronym, "(Central Military Remand Prison) buildings and who have since been forgotten."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does that paragraph go on to indicate that in fact approximately 2.000 of these prisoners or detained persons had been interviewed, none of whom were "interesting from the standpoint of crime"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there anything further indicated in this document as to whether the military police were responsible for the handling of these persons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further down in the same page, at the very bottom they state, according to the military police who met there, apparently, that it was the duty of the Department of Justice to appoint a warden and to make all the decisions in regard to these detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go next to Exhibit P 04756. Can you tell us -- sorry. Can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the minutes of a meeting held on the 2nd of September, 1993, at 9.00 in the morning. And in English it's called a meeting of the heads of the Defence Department, and I'm not positive, but I believe this is what, in B/C/S, they would call a kolidzija or a collegium of the top of a department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which would be the department head and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from the department head and his assistants, does this indicate that the deputy chief of the HVO of the Main Staff also attended?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the place of the commander of the HVO Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, as of September -- early September, 1993, who was the Deputy Chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if at that point it was Tole. He was later. Oh, no, it would have been Mr. -- at this point it would have been Mr. Petkovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I'm not positive, because the terminology changes, or it's difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, just in passing, that very confusion is discussed in this document on pages 2 and 3 of the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going to spend our time on that now, given --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- the time.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, under number item 1, I'm sorry, Deputy Head of Staff was Mr. Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me direct your attention particularly to item number 3 on page 4. And does this involve a report by the military police administration and by Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It states in the middle of the -- well, in the beginning of the second paragraph, that Mr. Coric put forward some of the problems which the military police had been encountering. And at the bottom, it says -- well, in the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment, sir. Before you get to that, let's go back up. Does it say, "Following Coric's contribution, Head, Stojic, made the following propose"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the proposals he made was: "All changes to be made with respect to the organisation in all different services must be submitted by the next board meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then the next line?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the next line is Mr. Coric mentioning some of the problems of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I ask you, then, to skip the rest of that paragraph and go to the portion starting with "Military prisons ..."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Military prisons are another example of very bad work. The head took the floor and said: --" Closed quote for a second. I should explain that the head of the department at this point would be Mr. Stojic. Back to the quote, and it's in quotation marks in the document: "My opinion is that we have two military prisons, Heliodrom and the military prison at Ljubuski. As for the other places where detainees are held (Gabela and Dretelj), I do not consider them as military facilities and refuse to personally endorse the work of these institutions." Period, close the quotation marks in the original and close quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following that statement by Mr. Stojic, did the Assistant Minister for Security, Mr. Lucic, make a response to that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does. Mr. Lucic then responds at the beginning of the next page, and this is also in quotes: "I believe that we cannot just pass over the problem of the Gabela and Dretelj prisons like that. That can cause us a lot of harm. We must say precisely who is behind these prisons, who is doing that, and what measures we can take with respect to that."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And following that discussion, can you just, in the interests of time, take us to -- was a conclusion then reached directing some further action to be taken?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conclusion reads: "The SIS, the Military Police Administration, and the Health Sector shall draft separate reports on the work of Dretelj and Gabela prisons and submit them to the Head of the Defence Department by Wednesday, 8 September 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I ask you, please, next to go to Exhibit P 03995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. You've just broached an interesting subject, and I'd like to get some specifics here. On the basis of the document that you've just read out and that you mention in your report as well, it appears that there are two types of prisons - military prisons and civilian prisons. The military prisons are Heliodrom and Ljubuski, and on the other hand, the more civilian prisons are Gabela and Dretelj. On the basis of what Mr. Coric says, he does not want to assume responsibility for the civilian prisons, if we can call them that, rather than the military ones. Now, if that is the case, your studies and your report, do they allow you to say who was in charge of Gabela and Dretelj? Under whose authority did they come if it was not under the authority of Mr. Coric? Who was it then? Allow the witness to answer first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I believe Mr. Coric first mentioned that military prisons were an example of bad work. Following that, Mr. Stojic voiced the opinion that only two of the prisons, the Heliodrom and Ljubuski - and he says in his opinion - were military, and the other two he did not consider to be military. Now, this is Mr. Stojic's opinion of the situation at this time, although as we'll see elsewhere in these documents, the persons involved can't necessarily agree as to who's responsible for what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, in the translation it says Stojic, but in the document is it Coric or Stojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just take a look quickly at the original. Yes, here we are. Now, in the original document, this appears at page 3. And I should note as well that the original document we have here, the pages were stamped out of order, but it's not a problem because there were page numbers at the top and you can reconstruct the correct order. Yes, there we are. If we go up to underneath the underlined section, it says that Mr. Coric is talking about the various problems of the military police, and Mr. Coric goes -- his speaking goes all the way down to the next paragraph, where he says there's also very poor work in the military prisons. And then the next thing that is said is that the floor is given -- the head of the department said -- or the floor was given to the head of the department, who said, and the quote which follows beginning with "I consider that we only have two military prisons" is the quote from Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who says "In my opinion," is it Coric or Stojic? "In my opinion," who says that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just check if I understand correctly. What then happens, it seems, is that Mr. Lucic said, "Watch it, hold it, we cannot leave this aside." And the fact that then reports are requested for Stojic I interpret as him having, to some extent, at least provisionally changed his mind and showing -- to be showing a preparedness to know better about Gabela and Dretelj also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's absolutely correct; that they decided in the end to look into these things, despite the initial opinion voiced by Mr. Stojic, because of the misgivings of Mr. Lucic, who was the Assistant Department Head for Security at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can then go to Exhibit P 03995, continuing with Mr. Stojic. Can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- I'm looking at the same one, I'm not sure. No, I'm not looking -- I'm looking at a different translation, but I believe it's the same document. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if you look, please -- if you have any doubt, look at what's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to look at the screen, yes. Thank you. It's a Defence Department order, and I believe if I look at the bottom if I'm looking at the same translation, from Mr. Bruno Stojic. Yes, this is the same document, just a different numbered translation. Mr. Stojic issues an order to bring more control and order into the detention facilities, and that -- he orders that as at the 10th of August, and -- shall I read this out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, under "Order."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I hereby order: As of the 10th of August, 1993, a commission authorised by the Department of Defence is to take charge of all detention units and prisons in which prisoners of war and military detainees are held. It will be composed of the following: "1. Berislav Pusic - chief of the offices for exchanges, president."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, Mr. Tomljanovich, because of time. The other names the Judges will be able to see, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I have a question. We come here upon a term which we have, I think, encountered before, the meaning of which to me is not quite clear, and that is "military detainees." Persons detained by the military, whatever, or military persons in detention who are not POWs, or what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume that it does not mean prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since in this context they're separated as a separate category from prisoners of war. My assumption, although it's not defined here, is that these are detainees being kept by the military, most likely -- and most of them probably being men of military age who weren't necessarily military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could that not mean as well military detainees of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could. And as a matter of fact, now that you mention it, they did keep -- in all of the detention centres I believe there were still their own prisoners as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the question that Counsel Nozica wanted to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour, precisely, because that's what it says in the Croatian version, prisoners of wars and military detainees. And you intervened quite rightly, Your Honour, and said that the military detainees were in fact HVO members who may be in detention because they committed some crimes or misdemeanors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Although my colleague said that we needn't read the other names, but I do think that something should be said about those names, all the more so that some of the names are on the Prosecutor's list of witnesses for testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not going to -- sorry. I'm not going to use the two hours that I have to discuss that. If the Court wants to ask that, you certainly can, or if counsel wants to ask it during cross-examination, he can. But I'd like to use my time as wisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After listing the names of this working group, sir, can you indicate what the -- what instructions were given to this group, what it is they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second page it states that they're authorised and have the duty to make a list of all detained persons, classify them in categories, and -- and I'll quote directly from here on: "Place under its control all of the detention units or prisons and resolve the matters of functioning and securing, regulate the questions of release from prison, exchange of prisoners, et cetera." Well, no, "et cetera," that's a period for the abbreviation, I'm sorry. "And all other important questions related to the work and functioning of detention units and prisons."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stojic --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Period, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stojic then indicate who it was who was responsible for making sure this area was carried out -- excuse me, these matter, these directions were carried out?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he instructs wardens or commanders of detention units and prisons to follow the instructions and orders of this committee and to work according to the structure they prescribe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just draw attention to a lack of clarity in terminology, because the document speaks of commission, commission, commission, and then suddenly we find the term "command." Is there a difference also in the B/C/S, and how is it to be explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where is it you see the word "command"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the last paragraph before "forwarded to." It says: "They must carry out the command's instruction." I read this "command" as referring to the commission, in fact. And is it called command suddenly because it has power to give orders or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me see what it says in the Croatian. In Croatian, it -- they use the word "komisija" consistently, that the directors and commanders of detention units and prisons are duty-bound to carry out the orders of the commission or to work under the scheme set forward by the commission. So "commission" is used quite consistently in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With due respect I contradict. I find the word "komisija" once in this last paragraph, at the end. And at the end of the English text I also find the word "commission". This is the line above. It must be a different -- "napitusa" -- no, it's also "komisija".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's also consistent in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you're an expert on HVO structures. Now we're dealing with structures here. We're dealing with the structures of the prison, in fact. And this document establishes a commission composed of a number of members, and according to the document, it seems that this commission exerts control over the detention facility. And the last paragraph seems to indicate that this commission issues commands, instructions, orders to the commanders of the prison. Now, if we look at structure here, if we look at the structure, the institution, isn't there an ad hoc commission in charge of controlling what is happening in the prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean prior to this order or as a result of this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Afterwards, as a result.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it would be this commission. Mr. Stojic is authorising them to -- he's transferring these powers to this commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that Mr. Stojic is transferring his powers to this commission, but the director or warden of the prison, is he placed under the control of the commission? I'd like to hear from the expert what he thinks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspect, given the wording of the very final paragraph, that it was Mr. Stojic's intention that the commission -- that the various directors of the various detention facilities follow the orders and instructions of this commission. Now, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're subordinate to them in the hierarchical structure, but he's giving them the authority to give orders to and establish new structures to this particular commission, and their authority has -- in those areas which he outlines, it has to be respected by -- their authority has to be respected by the various commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Judges will have an opportunity of going back to that question in due course. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, can you tell the Judges, during this period of time, as of August and early September of 1993, did you find anyone, any organisation or person within the HVO structure, who was willing to take responsibility for what was happening at these camps?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we go next to Exhibit P 04841.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Scott does that, the last -- the last question he put to the witness is one that clearly calls for a legal conclusion on the part of the witness which he's not qualified to give, and it's -- it's simply not a proper question to put somebody -- to somebody who's simply analysing documents, Your Honour, to put -- the Court is quite capable of reading these documents and drawing its own legal conclusions, and I would ask that the question and answer be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll rephrase the question if that's -- if that's necessary. I believe that he can, in fact, what Mr. -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges saw the question. They saw Mr. Murphy's intervention. So we will take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, in light of Mr. Murphy's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your review of the documentation, did you come across any senior HVO official or body which was -- who stood up -- of which stood up and took responsibility for what was happening in these camps at that time? If you remember such a document --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. No one takes full responsibility. People undertake actions to do something about the situation, but no one says explicitly "The full responsibility is ours," as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that in mind, please, can we then go to P 04841.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And tell us, first of all, what that is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the minutes of a working meeting of the -- well, now they're starting to call it the cabinet of the HR HB, or the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6 September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Both Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic are at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic are both at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Would you go to the bottom of page 1 under what says "Ad.", A-d period, "1.1" and reads what follows?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "To 1. On the basis of verbal reports and insights gained into the manner of executing punishments and the conditions of detention of persons captured as active-duty and reserve enemy forces and persons preparing an armed rebellion, the situation was deemed unsatisfactory --" or sorry, "declared unsatisfactory and harmful to the reputation and interests of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "It was also concluded that the responsibility for the present situation does not lie with the HVO of the HZ HB (Government of the HR HB). However, in order to avoid the situation being used in ways that are adverse to the political and other interests of the HR HB, valid principles of International Law of War and International Humanitarian Law need to be observed in executing punishments and implementing other measures."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, does the document then go on to reach certain conclusions, a list of, I believe, three conclusions, as to what should be done or what should follow from this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and specific persons are tasked with specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you to go through all of them, but if I can ask you to look at one example, to point number 3.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I read the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "3. In order to improve the conditions of accommodation and diet of detainees, the Office for Expelled Persons, Refugees and Displaced Persons is tasked to ensure the necessary quantities of food, personal hygiene items, and, if possible, equipment and material needed for accommodation (blankets, mats, et cetera)."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask you to look at P 05104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that time is precious, but I want to go back to this document. I want to have another look at the paragraph before the conclusion "At the same time ..." Could you read out that paragraph, the one that you haven't read out yet, but please read it out because it seems to be of interest and in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "At the same time, distinction needs to be made between penal and correctional organisations for the detention of persons subject to criminal proceedings or persons against whom a final judgement has been pronounced (military and civilian prisons), and centres for the detention of prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have read out this paragraph. You have examined it. You have studied it. As an expert of such structures, what sort of conclusion did you arrive at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion I arrived at was, reading this, also following what we saw earlier with the meeting of the kolidzija of the Department of Defence, that it wasn't clear to the people in the areas of the highest responsibility -- or there wasn't a clear distinction made, despite the fact there should have been according to laws, there was not a clear distinction made between facilities which were penal or correctional facilities in which persons are kept for criminal reasons and other persons, prisoners of war. So they were detaining prisoners of war and -- and prisoners, criminal prisoners, in the same prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Does this alternative not show that they forget about the whole category, namely, what we had before, the military detainees? They are neither/nor. It seems to be a document which is not based on full information of the local situation and categories.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, absolutely. And if we go to a later document, the meetings which I cite in December of 1993, still then, over three months later, there's still a great deal of confusion as to who is actually in the detention centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In one of the documents we've looked at before, amongst other things, somebody was charged with drawing a list of all detainees. Was that list actually drawn? Did you come upon it in your studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of lists. The one I know I've seen personally, because I found that one in the archive, I believe someone had drawn up lists of all the prisoners in Dretelj around this time; I believe there's a lists of prisoners in Heliodrom I've seen around this time, listed by hangar; and I believe then again in December, when these meetings are held which I cite in my report, there's more lists of prisoners which are being made, although I'm not sure whether I've seen the lists that were made in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When compiling your report, did you examine the legal situation that concerned civilian prisoners with respect to the penal code, the Criminal Code of Herceg-Bosna? Is this an issue you examined? Is this a question you posed, or is it an issue you didn't deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't deal with it other than that I'd seen quite a bit of information that persons had been detained without charges being filed. But that's not a question I deliberately went out and gathered information on. I should add there that with the camps, there's a great deal of documentation, and I very deliberately limited what I looked at by level of documentation, because otherwise it would be just too large of a task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can look briefly, then, at Exhibit P 05104. And if you have that, can you please tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of Mate Boban, signed and stamped on the 15th of September, 1993, which was forwarded to the Defence Department and the Main Staff of the HR HB armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of the current topic, if I could just direct your attention to item number -- paragraph number 3 on the second page of the English translation. Does Mr. Boban there address, again, the issue of the detention of prisoners and others and conditions of such detention?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both in -- in the second part of the order, Mr. Boban orders the military to carry out -- observe the standards of international humanitarian law when in combat, and in section 3, he orders that in those areas in which the conditions required by international law are not met, they should immediately be met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit P 05503. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Witness, to tell me, since in the previous chapter I notice -- it disappeared, by I saw there a particular paragraph which spoke about the necessity that the observers of the International Red Cross are to be allowed to visit the camps. And now I cannot in a way quote it because I do not have it here, but I believe it was the same thing. And now I would like to ask you if you have seen any other document in which reference was made to the possibility or kind of not giving the chance to the observers of the ICRC to visit the camps. That is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue of accessibility to camps, I just know from my previous work and from other trials that that was a very burning issue which was discussed quite a bit in the summer and fall of 1993. Now, as to the specifics of who was allowed to visit and exactly when, that's something I just didn't look at documents for in making this report. Other than the ones which we've just cited regarding the visit in August of 1993 to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then look, please, at P 05503. And can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report of a three-member commission which was part of the health care sector of the Defence Department of the HVO reporting on the sanitary conditions and medical conditions in the Heliodrom on the 30th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we see there eight conclusions on the second page of the English translation at least?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do those observations indicate - again, we don't have time to go through each one - a number deficiencies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number, many of which were already described in a previous exhibit. And this also adds more specifics as to the sanitary situation and the health situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention to the last page of the document. Can you just indicate a number of the people who received this or --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- or to whom this report was directed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This report was directed - and you'll need to scroll down a little bit more - first of all, to Mate Boban, then to Bruno Stojic, and then also to the General -- or Brigadier Zarko Tole. I believe that's Tole and not Tolo. And then the head of the health sector, Mr. Bagaric. And here it says Mr. Berko Pusic, although sometimes his first name is called Berislav and sometimes it's Berko. And then to the commander of the Heliodrom and then to the chief of the 3rd Brigade's medical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you next to go to Exhibit P 05812. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it 5812 or 5821?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is 5812.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you don't have it, please direct your attention to the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do. I just have it mislabelled. Yes. This letter is from the commander of the Heliodrom prison, Stanko Bozic, to Mr. Stojic and forwarded to Zarko Tole, as well as Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dated?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dated the 11th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, please direct your attention particularly to the opening paragraph, first of all. In stating his concerns, does Mr. Bozic indicate the time period encompassed by the problems he's raising?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says that these difficulties and problems have -- regard the persons who have been brought in since the 30th of June, 1993, brought in as detainees since the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does Mr. -- the Heliodrom warden, Mr. Bozic, indicate he's listing all of the problems or only the most serious problems?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says that he's only highlighting the ones that are top priority right at the moment, so only the very most important problems, of which there are eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One, number 1, and I'm not going to go in detail except to direct some of your attention to some of the questions put by the Judges earlier, but is item 1 the use of detainees for work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could you go to number 2?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2 or 1(B)?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Number 2?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2 is the severe wounding and other sufferings of the detainees. And, again, further down it mentions the same visits of the International Red Cross back on the 10th, 11th and 12th of August, 1993, in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of the letter, does Mr. Bozic give any indication, again, whether he as commander of the prison, if you will, or the warden is able to still, by now the middle of the October, 1993, is he able to solve these problems?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And, as a matter of fact, his last sentence in the letter reads: "As I am not able to solve these problems alone, I appeal to you to use your influence for these problems to be solved."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I next ask you, please, to go to Exhibit P 07064. And can you tell us what that is when you have it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to say that I'm afraid that the author of this document is on the list of the Prosecution's witnesses. So Mr. Tomljanovich is talking about this document rather than the author. You have instructed us and said that documents should be presented through the authors. I don't object to having this document shown to Mr. Tomljanovich, but I think we should exclude any other form of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's quite clear for the Chamber that when the witness reads out a paragraph, he's only reading out something that someone else drafted. He didn't draft it, so he is not expressing his opinion. Mr. Scott, with regard to this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us what that is, Mr. Tomljanovich?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have it in front of me, but I remember this one fairly well. This is a document from Mr. Biskic, who had just been made, fairly recently, assistant head -- or Assistant Minister of Defence of the HR HB. And this is a letter of the 7th of December, 1993, written to the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Gojko Susak, regarding the prisoners of war and the problems with prisoners in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. Do you have any more information on Mr. Biskic's background and where he had come from prior to being named an Assistant Minister of Defence in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was an officer of the Croatian army, the HV, although I'm not -- I don't remember right now exactly in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know why he was reporting -- giving this report to the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia was interested in seeing -- understanding the situation with the problems of prisoners of war in Herceg-Bosna because it had become the problem of the Republic of Croatia because of international pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Again, because of time, does Mr. Biskic then in the opening paragraph say that, having taken up his duties, he was able to immediately observe problems with the prisoner of war "shelters and collections centres"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And describes these problems as very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does he indicate in the letter the organisation or part of the HVO, based on his observations, who were responsible or had jurisdiction over the detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He makes the observation - I don't have it in front of me - but he makes the observation, I believe, that the Defence Department or Defence Ministry has been given responsibility, although he does not think that should have -- its overall responsibility, although he does not think that should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we scroll down on the document, please. Is that indicated in the last paragraph on that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I should make clear here that what we see in the last paragraph, where it says "MO HR HB", that's the Ministry of Defence. That's the Croatian -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the top of the next page, is there a heading called "Main Omissions"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then does he go on at the bottom of that page, carrying over to the last page of his letter, to propose a number of actions or steps?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention particularly to point number 4. Can you tell the Judges -- or read that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read that. Point number 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the highest level of the RH ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "RH" being whom?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RH being the Republic of Croatia. "... influence HR HB institutions to make them resolve the problem of detained persons as soon as possible in order to change the world's opinion of us, because representatives of the International Red Cross and the UN know the situation in the collection centres and the KRZ very well."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the attachment to that document, which is at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- I have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It strikes me that in -- unless I'm in error, in the documents you have shown us and the passages that have been pointed out to us, the problem of detainees was always regarded as being a problem because it seemed to damage, on the international level, the reputation of the HVO or later the HR HB. Now, did you come upon any documents where the concern was of a humanitarian motivation, someone showing some kind of concern for the personal fate of the persons concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in any of the documents I reviewed for this report. However, in open-source documents and press releases, that's frequently stated as a reason for intending to close the camps in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look at the attachment. One of the Judges earlier had a question about whether lists were prepared. Attached to this particular document is something titled "List of Detainees from the Heliodrom who Live in Mixed Marriages," which then goes on to list approximately 66 detained persons. From your research, sir, were you able to -- can you provide the Judges any assistance into the purpose of this list or the significance of listing only those detainees who lived in mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, persons who were to be released were sent either to territory controlled by the ABiH, sent to third countries via the Republic of Croatia, or allowed to stay in Herceg-Bosna. And persons of mixed marriages were a category which I believe, in general, were people allowed to stay, although I don't know anything about the fate of these particular people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you next to go to P 07096.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. On the list that you have before you, we can see the names of the men detained. They are to the left. And we have the dates of birth, and to the right we have the names of their wives, because Mr. Jusic Emir seems to be married to Sremer Kornelija, who is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's "H" and then we have "S" for Serbs. What does "H" represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be Croats, because it would be "Hrvati" or "Hrvatica" , in the original Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the "S" means the persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Srbi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can please go, then, to Exhibit P 07096, and tell us what that is, the significance of that document in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very quickly, this is an order or a decision of Mate Boban, signed on the 10th of December, 1993, to order the immediate closing of all detention centres in HR HB unilaterally and to implement this decision no later than the 17th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can then go back -- we looked at this yesterday, but if we can then look briefly again at P 07668. If you have that, can you remind us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have a copy of that. Here we go. Yes. This is, once again, the order or the decision of Mr. Prlic to nullify his earlier decision to open Gabela camp and to appoint its director.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the date of this decision closing the Gabela camp is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's December. If we could scroll down. Yes, 22nd of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the final two documents on the topic of camps. Could you look, please, at P 07124. And what is that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the minutes of a meeting for a working group for implementing Mr. Boban's order, which we just saw a minute ago, or his decision, and they're meeting on the 11th of December, 1993, in Posusje, under the chair of Colonel Marijan Biskic, an order to enact this order to close the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, by this date in December, the Minister of Defence is listed as Mr. Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had Mr. Stojic stopped being the Minister of Defence by that time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had. In the HR HB, Mr. Perica Jukic, for a few months only, was the Minister of Defence of the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of other persons present at the meeting, did they include the wardens of the Ljubuski, Gabela, and Heliodrom camps?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do. As well as military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it also -- do the list of attendees also include Mr. Berislav Pusic, towards the end of the list?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. As well as dignitaries from -- at least one dignitary from the republic of -- oh, I'm sorry. Forget I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to page number 3 of the report, or the minutes. Excuse me. Could I direct your attention to the second paragraph and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that Mr. Ibrisimovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My objection is this: Since Mr. Scott mentioned all the functions of the persons here but he seems to have skipped Mr. Pusic, he did not -- was not present as president of the commission but, when we look at the document 3995, I think, the document we saw a moment ago, was the president of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The documentation will show, and I would think there would be no dispute, that Mr. Pusic was wearing a number of hats during this time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But let's be precise here. At that meeting on the 30th of December, 1993, Mr. Pusic was there, and I see him written down as head or president of the prisoners of war exchange office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention to the second paragraph on page 3 in reference to, in fact, Mr. Pusic. Could you read that paragraph to us, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "After Colonel Biskic's introductory remark, Mr. Berislav Pusic took the floor and informed those present that at this moment in the HR HB there are detention centres operating in Capljina, Gabela, Mostar, Heliodrom, Tomislavgrad, in the town itself and in Sujica, Livno, Prozor and Ljubuski. He said at this point he did not have a precise figure, because until now detainees were constantly being taken away to work, mostly on the preparation of the front line."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is -- excuse me, please. There is one mention I don't understand. "In the town itself," what does that refer to? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's in regard to Tomislavgrad, which is a town and a municipality. So there was a camp in the town of Tomislavgrad and also in Sujica, which is a town, I think, in the municipality of Tomislavgrad, north of Tomislavgrad. So there were two camps in the municipality; one was in the seat of the municipality; one was in this smaller town, Sujica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. But we have to break there. We've been working for more than an hour and a half. It's 10 to 4.00. We'll reconvene at 10 past 4.00. Mr. Scott, you've roughly used an hour and a half so far. How much more time do you need? Because theoretically you have just 30 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Our records, Your Honour, which I understand confirm or are consistent with the registry that so far I have used 57 minutes, so I have approximately one hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll reconvene at 4.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed, but the Judges have a question to ask the witness before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, I return to the order Mate Boban gave on December 10th that all prisoners be released by December 17th. We have then seen an order signed by Mr. Prlic on the 23rd, more or less but certainly after the 17th, concerning the closure of Gabela. Can you tell the Bench how the order given by Mate Boban was actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in large part, the order was implemented through these two meetings which we're introducing right now where all of these matters were discussed. It was also implemented through the decision closing Gabela. Now, as far as when or how Mr. Boban's order was received by Mr. Prlic, that I don't know because we don't have that documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Were all prisoners actually released by December 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I believe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And the last question: Was Mate Boban competent to order such release according to the HR HB constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no constitution. I just want to make sure that's very, very clear. There is no constitution. There is no state. There maybe something else, but there's no constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: When you say there is no state, that's part of your pleading, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no. There's no constitution. If there is a constitution and if the Trial Chamber believes there is a constitution, I would like to see it. But there's no constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document that organises the quasi-statelet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If that's the Trial Chamber's position at this point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm asking a question. I'm not stating a position, Mr. Karnavas. And I think the witness can answer if I reduce it to asking: Was Mate Boban legally competent to pass such an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but the moment that you're calling it a quasi-statelet it would appear to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I've withdrawn that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm asking if Mate Boban was competent to pass such an order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's -- that's a legal question. I think if you read his powers as commander-in-chief broadly and his authority over the Department of Defence, he would be, although I imagine you could make an argument that he would not have been. But I really don't know, according to the laws of the HR HB at the time, or according to the various basic decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in order to complete the question raised by Judge Trechsel with respect to the closing of the prisons, you explained to us the different categories of the detainees that were in those prisons, and we took note that there were prisoners of war as detainees and military detainees. Now, when the order came to close all the prisons, what was the situation, the juridical, the legal situation with respect to the military detainees who had committed offences? What happened to them? Were they set free or were measures taken to place them in detention in other prisons, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although that's something I haven't looked at in this report, I know there was, generally speaking, the intention at this time to raise charges against anyone who was intended to be kept in detention. I also know that, just from looking through the archives and finding documents, charges were raised quite frequently by local prosecutors against various persons who were in detention. But I don't know if everyone who was still in detention had charges filed against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This decision by Mate Boban that you pointed out, did you look at the preamble and the motives for the decision that was taken? How do you interpret, you as an expert in the structure of the Herceg-Bosna, how do you explain the fact that he's going to motivate that by referring to the fact that peace can only exist through freedom? Does that mean that freedom means liberating all the prisoners, setting them free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's certainly the implication given what order -- or what the decision is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps during the cross-examination we'll come back to that at some point. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, on that point, sir, the preamble if you will, as the President calls it, to Boban's order, can you tell the Judges whether you have any information whether that language was simply meant for international public consumption?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was certainly a public document, I would imagine, so I would imagine this wording was. And it's also remarking on the day of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Once again I'm going to object to asking this witness to speculate about the intentions of other parties of which he can have absolutely no knowledge whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question should have been put in the following way: To the best of the witness's knowledge as an expert, on the basis of -- did the decision have a public character or was it a confidential decision that was taken? So it's on the basis of your work that you can -- that you can answer that question. On the basis of your research, was the document something that was known publicly? Did they discuss it or did anybody know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly known publicly, and this particular document, I believe, was found in the HVO archive, in the Croatian archive in Zagreb. So it was -- I don't know off the top of my head in whose papers it was found, but -- and there isn't a circulation list, but if there's no circulation list, it would probably be intended for broad public distribution if nobody's specified specifically as being the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
