utterances.text: If we can continue back to finish up on Exhibit P 07124. We were previously looking before the break at page 3. Can I direct your attention, please, over to the top of page 4, and simply to note that for the Chamber at that part of the document Mr. Pusic and Mr. Bozic provide some information as to the number of prisoners in the various detention camps.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do, and their figures are widely divergent. They spend some time arguing over the actual number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this is the day after -- this is the 11th of December, the day after Mr. Boban's order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we go on, then, please, to Exhibit P 07143. I'm sorry. 7143. If I -- I may have said 74 -- there's both, but this is 7143. Can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it as 7413 here, but it's the same document. It's the minutes of the next meeting which followed after the last meeting we've seen on 13th of December, 1993. They've been charged with making lists and categorising prisoners and coming back to this meeting, and there are some of the same persons, although some persons are attending here for the first time. It's still a very large meeting. And -- yeah. This is still in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And among the list of those attending, does it also include Mr. Berislav Pusic listed here in the English language as head of the Office for the Liberation of Captured and Missing Persons in the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to the next page of the document, page 3. And did Colonel Biskic indicate four steps or actions that were needed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, in the middle of the page, that it was necessary to decide who was permitted to remain in the HR HB. In regards to prisoners of war, persons responsible were supposed to be the military police and the SIS, which is military counter-intelligence. They're going to set a deadline for those with responsibility for those leaving to third countries, these prisoners being left out. And finally, to make a deadline for those with responsibility, for those who wish to cross over to the -- well, here it says "Muslim side" but ABiH-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we go on to other parts of the document, does the next paragraph indicate that as of December of 1993 there were still women being held at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And I believe in the previous document as well, I think it was Mr. Lucic who made reference to that, that the women should be released first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as we flip through the document, and starting on page 4, do we then begin to get a series of numbers per camp, the total number of persons in the camp, and then what is going to -- the disposition of the various persons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do. It's divided by camps, and numbers are given for how many can stay in the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's just start with Mostar on page 4, just as one illustration. We won't do the others. But what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see here. This first set of -- you mean the ones after number 1? Heliodrom, Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- down there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Out of a total of 1.896, 24 could stay in the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 240, sorry. 369 would remain in prisons and isolation, and 491 would be transferred across the lines to ABiH-held territory, and 203 would be transferred to a third country. This is just this subgroup of prisoners they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did your research show, in terms of this last group being transported to a third country, by what mechanisms were these people going to be transferred out, outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, to some other country?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, when people were transferred to third countries, they first had to obtain a visa for a third country and then were given free -- free passage through Croatia, the Republic of Croatia. Frequently as well, people were sent to camps in the Republic of Croatia. I know there was one large one -- one important one in Korcula, and then they'd be transferred to third countries from there. Generally speaking, they wouldn't be sent to Croatia until a third country agreed to take these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can then just direct your attention to page 10, to one final item in this document. On page 10, again, generally, under the heading for the Heliodrom, we get a series of numbers, and then it says this: "743 persons were without category, and he proposed that they be handed over to the supervision of the International Red Cross." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you provide the Judges with any information as to exactly how that was going to work? Were they going to say, "Here, International Red Cross, you take care of them?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this commentary, Your Honour. I know I'm dealing with professional Judges, but at some point an Appeals Chamber may be reading the record, and I don't think it's very helpful to have the Prosecutor leading the witness or making these sort of flip comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Tomljanovich, do you have any information about how it was that this would be handled, implemented, carried out, that they would -- that 743 persons would be "handed over to the supervision of the International Red Cross"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With these particular persons, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can I use this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- natural break to return to the list of the persons taking part in this meeting, and especially the qualities ascribed to Mr. Pusic. "Head of the Office for the Liberation of Captured and Missing Persons in HR HB". Now, I don't know how you liberate missing persons. That's one question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I haven't heard about this office before either. Was this an office that was created as a consequence of this order of 10 December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't necessarily believe so. If I could see that page in the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Let's see here. Where is Mr. Pusic here? It's near the top. Oh, I see here, yes. Uh-huh. Yes. He's listed here as being the chief of the Office for the Liberation of Prisoners and Displaced Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we just go back to the practice that you can read it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- if you can read it in the B/C/S and get the interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] "The Head of Office for the Liberation of Captured Persons and Missing Persons in the HR HB."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I got this, yes. But still, since when does this office exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it doesn't. And it may be incorrect terminology for his title as the -- the head of the office for exchange and -- exchange of prisoners and other persons. That's always a possibility, that the terminology was wrong from whoever took the notes. That particular wording I don't think I've ever seen in any other document, although I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Leaving the topic of camps, can you tell us -- on one of our final topics, can you tell us what the relationship or powers of the HVO HZ HB were in relation to the municipalities, and whether there were any decrees or decisions setting that relationship out?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both in the basic decision on executive government and that on municipal government, it's made clear that the HVO HZ HB has the right and the duty to nullify any local legislation which is not in accordance with general law or general ordinances or general policy, and that this particular power was used a number of times in 1992 and 1993. There's also a power of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does the power of appointment also include a power of dismissal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you to look, please, at Exhibit P 00250. When you have that, can you tell us what it is and very quickly point out to us the most pertinent sections or language relevant to --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's the statutory decision on municipal executive government. This is already -- this is back from June of 1992. I don't have -- let's see here. No. It's printed in the Narodni List of September, but it was from -- it was approved -- here I am. I have it. 13th of June, 1992, and signed by Mate Boban. And the relevant articles which you were talking about are number -- Article 6, in particular, which reads: "The HVO HZ HB shall supervise the legality of the municipal HVO's work. "The HVO HZ HB shall issue compulsory instructions to the HVO in its competence."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're reading from Article 6 now? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention back up to Article number 2.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Article number 2 says that the president -- sorry, I'll quote: "A president, office heads, and other of its members which shall appointed and dismissed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna Croatian Defence Council, hereinafter HVO HZ HB, shall make up the municipal HVO." So that gives the HVO the power of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could we next go, please, jumping from one end of the documents to the other, but to Exhibit P 09530, a document that we also saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the Rules of Procedure of the HVO HZ HB, which we saw yesterday, from the 12th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And these were issued or signed by Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention specifically to page 14, Articles -- well, actually starting on page 15, Articles 39 through 41, do those, again, set out the relationship and powers and responsibility of the municipalities -- the municipal HVOs in relationship to the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do. And, again, in Article 40 they state that -- and here's the quote in the second paragraph: "If the municipal HVO fails to act in conformity with the preceding paragraph, the HVO HZ HB shall act in conformity with Article 15 of the statutory decision on the provisional organisation of executive power and administration in the territory of the HZ HB ..." Which is yet another order. It's the provisional order. I'm sorry, did I remember to close the quote? Yes. That is yet another order. I think the revised one is earlier. But there's three orders now where this is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or three decisions or decrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you for the witness to be shown, from the organisational charts, Exhibit P 09689, page 3 on the charts. Third chart. Could be page 4 in e-court, I'm told, but the third chart. Now, can you look at that, sir, and does that chart indicate the relationship or structure between the HVO HZ HB and the municipal HVOs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This chart is very general and generic. You see at the top, the HVO HZ HB with the various department heads, president and vice-presidents; in between, you have, cited here again, the power of appointment from Articles 13 and 15 of the statutory decision on executive government; and Article 13, the right to nullify -- the right and duty to nullify acts contrary to the general interest. And at the bottom here we have a generic municipal HVO structure. The idea in general was that every department and many subdepartments would have local offices in each municipality, although, depending on the municipality and its size, they may combine quite a number of these functions into one office. So in each municipality, the number of members was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before going on, just to inject the idea that the municipal HVOs, could they also issue orders and decrees on a municipal basis?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could and they did, and at least large municipalities like Mostar had their own Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just as one example of that, could I ask you to go to P 05039. Yes. There's actually several -- two decisions here. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me. I don't have it in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask you to go to the second page of the English translation, to the second decision indicated in the document. 24th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is that about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the decision to prohibit the work of the Party of Democratic Action, or the SDA, which was the leading Muslim party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, within Mostar municipality. And we don't have it yet on the translation, but I believe it also characterises the party as a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've said that -- looked at these statutes and decisions, decrees, that there was the power to nullify, that the central government, if you will, the HZ HB, had the authority to nullify decisions. Did you come across any examples of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I came across a handful of examples, I think most of which were in Narodni List as early, I think, as the late summer/fall of 1992, and at least as late as May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, before turning to one of those, to look at Exhibit P 00788. And as soon as you have that, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it. This is a letter which I believe was -- I think this was a paket radio. I'm not sure. It was received on the 21st of November, 1992. We only have the receipt here dated, and it's to all HVO HZ HB municipal presidents from Jadranko Prlic. It's in regards to contact with representatives of UNPROFOR, and he's instructing them that all such contacts should be made only following the consultation and coordination with the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask you next to look at P 02248. Can you tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a decision on the invalidation of a decision which had been made by the municipality of Mostar on the 24th of March, 1993, which I believe is signed by Mr. Prlic. And the decision was in relation to the mobilisation of material within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could turn, please, to the last topic, and that is the formation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the HR HB. Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit P 04611. Please tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe if we could go to the -- I don't have this in front of me. I believe this is the declaration -- if we could scroll down in the B/C/S and go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Yes. This is the basic decision on the establishment and declaration of the HR HB, which is signed, I believe, here by the head of the Assembly, Mr. Perica Jukic, on the 28th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In the interests of time, if I can just direct your attention in particular to Article 11 -- Articles 11 and 12. What does Article 11 provide?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 11 provides that until there is a constitution and that it's -- until the constitution and all of the bodies -- yes, here we are. "Until such time as the constitution and the bodies of the HR HB are established, the HZ HB institutions shall still be applied, as shall regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina if they are not in contravention with the regulations of the HR HB."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for accuracy's sake, when you say "the regulations of the Republic --" does it say "the regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" or "the regulations of --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. "Former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what does Article 12 provide?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 12 provides that: "Until such time as elections are held and the bodies of state authority are appointed, in accordance with the provisions of this decision, the duties of state authority shall be performed by the bodies of the authority of the HZ HB." And the president shall remain the same as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go to the organisational chart, P 09689.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but in Article 11 there's been a mistranslation again, and I'm surprised to see that this was not mentioned by the witness. It mentions the republic that has existed to date and not the former republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the article, Article 11, in the B/C/S version and we will listen to the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 11. [Interpretation] "Until such time as the constitution of the republic is adopted and the bodies of the republic are established, the regulations in force for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be applied in the territory of the Republic, as shall the regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that has existed to date if they are not in contravention of the regulations of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you now to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The word "dosadsanji" is a little ambiguous and could be interpreted in both ways, either as "former" or "to date."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can ask that the witness be shown, as part of Exhibit P 09689, the organisational charts, the chart on page 2, or maybe page 3 in e-court. Chart 2. Page 3. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is this a chart that's been prepared to show the relationships of these bodies similar to the one we looked at on Monday but after the HR HB was established?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an organigramme of the HR HB, and it is very similar to the organigramme we saw of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, can you tell the Judges, apart from the changing of names and labels - such as instead of "department" now they're "ministries"; instead of "president", "prime minister" - were there any significant changes in the actual operations and functions of these bodies between the HZ HB and the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on what you consider significant. There's a great deal of continuity. I can outline just very briefly the major changes which were made --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which, to large degree, are nomenclature. And I should add that names are finally -- the names in HR HB are catching up to what had actually been the practice, and they're more descriptive names of these bodies than the names in the HZ HB had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, for example, in the left upper portion of the chart what had been - we discussed this quite a bit - the HZ HB Presidency is now called the House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It fulfils a very similar legislative role. There is a great degree more legislation in stating how it should operate. The members are expanded and redefined, and they did then meet more regularly than the Presidency. But their powers are very, very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask that the witness be shown the -- Exhibit 4, it may be page 5 in e-court, of that bundle of charts. No, I'm sorry, one -- my apology. The one before that. Is this, sir, an updated chart, if you will, again showing the relationship between the central government and the municipals after the creation of the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And, once again, this is highly simplified and generic. It doesn't describe any particular municipality. But, once again, we've listed the sections of the laws which apply to dismissal and supervision of municipal governments and the duty to nullify legislation. Now, the main difference is that many of the duties which had been subdepartments in the HZ HB become full ministries. Another difference, which really isn't of much consequence to the period we're talking about, is the law did foresee the possibility of creating elected municipal assemblies which would then elect municipal -- municipal governments, although this was only to be done at such time when the conditions permitted, and I don't believe that was done anyplace during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before we leave -- I'm sorry, if we could go back to the previous chart. I believe it's chart number 2 of the overall book, which, again, may be page 3 in e-court. Just finishing up with this. On this chart, which is different than the HZ HB chart, to the right of Mate Boban there is a box that says "Presidential Council."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please explain that development to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Mate Boban left the position as president of HR HB, he wasn't appointed by one man but by --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or replaced.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. You're right. He wasn't replaced by one man, he was replaced by a collective body which was presided over by Kresimir Zubak, and the other members of the collective Presidency are listed here. And the basic decisions were modified on that day in order to allow for such an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, if we can look at P 06776 or -- actually, 6776 and 6995 are basically the same document. Let's use 6995, I'm sorry, because that's the one actually out of the Gazette. P 06995. And does that indicate the officers who are positions -- ministers who were elected or selected as a result -- after the change to the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. This comes from the 20th of November, 1993, and is signed by the brand new -- well, he's still the vice-president of the House of Representatives, Ivan Bender, and it's the election of the government or of the cabinet. In the HR HB, the president would nominate the government and the Assembly would elect them, and this is the election. And all the ministers are all here, as are the presidents and vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we let the witness go, I would like to tender the remaining documents. I didn't stop and do that as we went today, trying to move as quickly as possible, but I'll do that now. P 03673, P 03560, P 03565, P 04352, P 04756, P 03663, P 03995, P 04841, P 05104, P 05503, P 05812, P 07064, P 07096, P 07124, P 07143, P 00250, 0 -- sorry, P 09689, P 05039, P 00788, P 02248, P 04611, P 06995. And before I finish, Your Honour, I want to make it clear that the Prosecution is tendering, as explained on Monday, we're tendering the entire set of Narodni List documents for each of the relevant years 1992, 1993, and 1994, including the individual translated items that go with each bundle. And we're also tendering as a complete collection all of the records of the meetings of the HVO HZ HB. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now address the Defence. I hope you have reached an agreement and that it won't be necessary for the Chamber to decide as to how you should use your time. Who will start the cross-examination? Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I will be starting the cross-examination. Your Honour, it would be helpful if we could, once again, review the time that is available. I think that the Defence has made the necessary internal arrangements, but if it could be indicated exactly how much time we have, that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll be working until 7.00 p.m., and we have the entire day tomorrow, and we have Monday. We'll have perhaps have two additional hours, but that won't be on Tuesday. That will have to be on some other day. So you have two hours until 7.00 p.m., excluding the break, and then you have tomorrow and Monday. So you have eight hours. Four hours tomorrow, four hours on Monday, plus an hour or a half or two hours. That amounts to nine and a half hours. And perhaps you'll need two additional hours. So you have a total of eleven and a half hours, provided that there are no interruptions, no incidents, et cetera. I don't know how you have divided the time among yourselves. You have perhaps discussed the matter. Mr. Murphy, have you decided on how to share your time, or are you just going to proceed blindly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have -- we have made certain decisions about that which I may or may not have changed, as with certain counsel just since the last break because of what was asked in examination-in-chief. But for the moment my assumption is that we will be proceeding on the basis that Ms. Nozica and I have at least two hours. We expect that perhaps further time will be made available to us by one of the other accused, and that should become clear after the next break. I don't know whether there's any advantage in my rehearsing all of the arrangements that have been made, but suffice it to say that at this point we will assume that there will be no difficulties that arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we will all assume that there will be no difficulties arising. That's already quite positive. Mr. Murphy, you may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the usher's assistance, I wonder whether, if Mr. Scott has no objection, I could borrow the small podium he has there. The ones in the courtroom are really too big to be of practical use, if he doesn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tomljanovich.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: My colleague Ms. Nozica and I represent the accused Bruno Stojic. I'm sure you know that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you're aware, I think, of the need for -- for us to be slow because the interpreters have to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Also, I want to ask you if you have available a copy of your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I'd like you to feel free to refer to that as much as you wish. I will be asking you certain questions about it. I'd like to begin with your qualifications, which I have to say I find very impressive. One small point on that: You mentioned that you were -- held the position of a lecturer at both Yale and Dickinson universities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not exactly sure what my specific title was for each particular job I would get each semester. It would frequently change.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I just ask because there is a certain difference in terminology between academic positions in the United States and Europe, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. And also within institutions and between institutions in the United States as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If you had been a full-time member of the faculty at those universities, your style would have been that of an assistance professor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So, in fact, what it indicates is that you were essentially teaching on a part-time basis while pursuing advanced studies.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At Yale, indeed I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Dickinson I was teaching part-time because I had moved there in the middle of writing my dissertation while my wife had obtained a job there at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I see. Now, you're currently employed by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You've been employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, I think, since 1999?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, March 2nd, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And is that your -- has that been your only employment since 1999?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular employment, yes. I did receive money for the book which I had published as well as the two chapters in a book which I had published as well. But that was an outside activity and not actually employment, I wouldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you were not employed by or acting as an agent for anyone else other than the Office of the Prosecutor during that time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you've been presented, as you know, as an expert witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I'd like to just understand or to get your understanding of what exactly your field of expertise is that you have favoured us with in this case.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand your question could possibly mean two things; an expert in the legal sense that we're using it as an expert in the court, or just generally an expert, as somebody who knows a lot about a subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let me come at it a different way. You're a professional historian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And essentially your job within the Office of the Prosecutor makes use of that professional knowledge and experience, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And the research that you have done in this case you have done using your skills as an historian?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both my skills as an historian and the knowledge I've obtained on the job here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as an historian, Mr. Tomljanovich, would you agree with me that in conducting historical research one should look objectively at all sides of a given question?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In historical research, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me that in historical research one should have access to as many different sources as possible?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Once again, you have approached your work in relation to this case using your skills as an historian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using my skills as an historian but not necessarily the same approach, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that, but let's -- let's, first of all, examine your qualifications in a little more detail. I think we can agree that you're not a lawyer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not now, nor have I ever been a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You had never studied law either in the United States or in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I emphasise that because you've been asked a number of questions in examination-in-chief about the structures within the HZ HB and the HR HB, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And the answers that you've given, can we agree, are not intended to be statements of the law as regards the structures of those organisations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I think I made that clear in an earlier answer, that I can only tell you what the documents say; I can't tell you what legally -- legally was correct or incorrect within the system of law of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, I ask that because certain questions were put to you about the competence of certain persons or the way things were supposed to work. But just to make it clear, that's not something that you can really help with as a legal question?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a legal -- a legal question, although as a practical question, the function of government in Herceg-Bosna was followed by people who weren't lawyers as well. But, no, it's not a legal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it's also true that you're not a political scientist by training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you're not an economist by training?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Though you did in your examination-in-chief give us an extended discussion of inflation and hyperinflation in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but to make it clear, you're not a professional economist, are you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I had to spend Croatian dinars in this period and that is the basis of my knowledge, and I've also looked at exchange rates. But I'm not an economist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So your knowledge on that subject comes from spending Croatian dinars; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was living there at the time and I knew -- I mean, first of all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also for the Tuta-Stela trial, I prepared a list of the exchange rates between the Croatian dinar and the German Deutschmarks, the official rates going through, well, the entire period of the Croatian dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that this was the first time that you have given evidence as an expert witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I submitted -- I was put forward as an expert once before in the Kordic case, but I was not heard by the Bench in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Why was that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Judge May, at the time, said that my testimony was redundant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you have testified as a witness in the contempt hearing against Markica Rebic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Markica Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But in that case you did not testify as an expert?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, given that this was your first time as an expert witness, did somebody explain to you before you came to give evidence what the function of an expert witness is in legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in legal proceedings as far as what would be expected of me as an expert in a trial in the ICTY, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And who gave you that explanation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation was given both in broad terms by Mr. Scott as well as by my immediate supervisor, Mr. Patrick J. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: What did Mr. Scott and Mr. Treanor tell you the function of an expert witness was in legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in legal proceedings in general. They didn't tell me that in a broad theoretical legal framework, but they did tell me the sorts of things I'd be expected to do and the sorts of things I would not be expected to do as an expert here at the ICTY, based on prior experience of other expert testimony here at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, did they explain to you that the function of an expert witness is to provide the Court with an opinion on technical matters?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. Not in those words, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, then, perhaps you could tell us in your own words what your understanding is today of the role of an expert at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was instructed that my role was to put forward the evidence and reach any possible conclusions or make any possible statements I could based on the documentary evidence I had, rather than on my own personal opinions or on speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you were told that you weren't supposed to speculate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I was told that if I do speculate and if I am asked a question by the Bench or by other side and I can't answer it on the basis of documentation, I need to say so, and the Judges will either want to hear that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I see. So then in terms of looking at the documents, you do agree that it is your function to provide the Court with an opinion?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly speaking, yes, although I'm not necessarily sure I understand the legal implications of an opinion. But, broadly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Have you finished your answer, or were you --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was thinking about the answer still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. We --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say it depends on what you call an opinion. Certainly not an opinion based on my own personal thoughts but only opinions and conclusions which I can reach on the basis of the evidence which I have in front of me for this particular testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So could we summarise it, then, by saying this: That you would be asked to read the documents and provide commentary on them? Is that what it comes to, really?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, did Mr. Scott or Mr. Treanor explain to you that one of the attributes expected of an expert witness is to be neutral or objective?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you recall that, indeed, Judge Antonetti instructed you at the beginning of your evidence that you were now the witness of the Court?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, referring to your report for a moment, do you consider that to be a neutral and objective expert report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you consider the evidence that you have given so far to be neutral and objective?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about your employment with the Office of the Prosecutor. You said that your function was that you were a member of a leadership research team.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's called the Leadership Research Team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And at one point in your evidence you used the phrase "bringing documents in house," and I took that to indicate a certain pride in and identification with the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bringing them in house means going on mission, going through archives elsewhere and bringing them to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the function of the Office of the Prosecutor within the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Office of the Prosecution's function in the Tribunal is to carry out -- now, I can't remember the actual number of the UN Resolution, but to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to carry out the Statute and do its duties as outlined in the UN Resolution setting up the ICTY, and also to observe the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let's make it concrete. The Office of the Prosecutor conducts investigations; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Collects evidence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Identifies suspects?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Drafts indictments and presents them for confirmation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And then prosecutes the accused with the intention of obtaining convictions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's true for the OTP as one whole unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And you're an employee of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the investigations section of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your function is to help the Prosecution build its case before trial, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our function -- this should be made clear: Our function in the investigations section is to investigate what happened. It's the function of the lawyers in the Prosecution section to decide who then may or may not be legally responsible for something and to decide how the case should be argued or any cases should be argued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I understand, sir. How long have you worked on this present case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On and off - I haven't worked continuously on this certainly - on and off, I've worked on things related to this case - oh, boy - since -- probably since the first or second week since I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You worked on other cases involving Croatian and Bosnian accused as well, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Blaskic case was nearly done by the time I got here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so I was assigned to the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Tuta and Stela?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And based upon your researches over such a large number of years, you have a considerable knowledge now about the facts of these cases. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I'd have to warn you that a part of what's discussed in those cases, especially if we're talking about Tuta and Stela, I couldn't tell you very much about the crime base. Generally, my -- my involvement there was to help prepare for Defence witnesses, if they were persons of, you know, particular political or governmental importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about some of the things that you've done in this case. You took part in interviewing some people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In fact, you interviewed a Ms. Viherouria in October of 2001.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In December 2001, you actually were present and helped conduct an interview of the accused Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in January and February, 2004, you interviewed Mr. Zubak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Remind the Judges who Mr. Zubak is, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- initially he was a judge from Doboj in Northern Bosnia, and then he became the vice-president of the HVO HZ HB, particularly involved in questions of justice and legality. He was briefly the Minister of Justice in the HR HB, and then he became the president of the -- well, the president of the collective Presidency of the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is he a person who has been indicted in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Was that decision based, in part, upon the interviews that you've conducted?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you'd have to ask Mr. Scott and the other lawyers. The decision to indict or not indict is not my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way, then: Were you asked for and did you give advice as it whether Zubak should be indicted?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of his interview, I don't think we discussed that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you discuss it at some other time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the very early days of my work here when -- prior to -- you know, very early on, possible targets were discussed amongst a broad segment of people. Anybody who could conceivably have been responsible was looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about that, then. What you're telling us is, then, that you played a part in meetings at which it was discussed who might be indicted in the Tribunal and who would not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were meetings where very -- various possible targets and possible avenues of investigation were discussed. I was not there when it was discussed who specifically would be a target of a formal investigation. I was there discussing -- at meetings where possible indictments were discussed, though, after the formal investigations had been opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I understand that that was not your decision, sir, so my question, really, is just this: It would be reasonable to assume that your opinions were taken into account in making certain decisions as to who might be suspects and who should be indicted. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to know how seriously, you'd have to ask Mr. Scott and the other senior attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm really not concerned to know how seriously. I'm just asking whether it's reasonable for us to think that your opinion was taken into account.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as my opinions on what, in fact, happened, yes. I don't know if my -- I never expressed opinions saying, "Well, you could charge so-and-so for this and could charge so-and-so for that." But my opinions, when I was asked, for example, "What is in the Narodni List," and asked "What do these documents tell us," I've always told the Prosecution section what I thought about those things. And since they keep asking me, I presume they did take me seriously on those issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Other than interviewing these persons that we've discussed, did you play any other part in the investigation of the case against these accused?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, although it's not strictly directly, but one of the biggest duties I've had over the years I've been here is bringing in the documentation from archival missions and -- and dealing with materials which we were acquiring, many of which were used in this case, many more of which were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And as the evidence accumulated, did you attend strategy sessions or other meetings as to how the case should be developed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I would receive further tasks on which things needed to be researched further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Before the trial started in this case late in April, did you have any tasks in assisting the Prosecutors to prepare for trial?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This April?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Before the trial started, yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was working on this report. I was assigned to do this in November of 2005. However, I was working on another case till about February. So I was working on this report more or less steadily from February through April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you to look for sources of information outside the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's always occurring to us to look for more information from outside the office. We always would welcome more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the first day that you gave evidence, you said, and I can refer you to the transcript if you wish, that your approach to this case was really no different from that of an academic expert looking at these things from the outside. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I put it in those words. I believe -- I believe Mr. Scott asked me the question, "Would you have done anything differently were you not working for the Prosecution?" And I said, no, that my approach was the same as it would have been if I was from the outside. However, and I added, and this is certainly true, if I was coming from the outside I wouldn't have access to this much material, nor would I have had this much time to become familiar with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, I have the transcript here, and I'll just read to you what you said, if I may.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: This is, for the record, the transcript of the 4th of September, and I'm beginning at page 16, line 23. I'm beginning, really, in mid-sentence. Mr. Scott asked you: "... can you tell the Judges, sir, is there anything about your approach or the methodology of the work that you did in connection with your report or about observations that you have made in your report that in your view would be any different if you had performed this work while not employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?" And then your answer begins at page 17, line 6: "No, with one very clear exception. I can't imagine I'd be able to look at as much of this material and have as much time to get to know this much material as well if I hadn't been working here full time for seven and a half years. But other than that, I didn't reach -- I don't think -- if I'd been, say, an academic expert looking at these things from the outside, I can't imagine how it would have been any different or how my conclusions would have been any different ..." Now, sir, today you have agreed with me that for several years you played an active role in investigating this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You consulted with respect to many important decisions.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Some of which may have determined whether certain people became accused in this case or whether they did not.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure exactly how much my work contributed to who was indicted and who was not, especially in terms of amounts, although certainly it was -- it certainly was considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, as an historian, would you not agree with me that in looking at the history of any conflict one must treat with a little caution the opinions expressed by people who were actively involved in one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. In history you should treat it with caution, and in a trial you should probably treat it with even greater caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And your position, sir, in this case is not that of an academic expert but somebody who is intimately and deeply involved with one of the parties to the case. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. However, I was never told what sort of conclusions I should reach. I was only given the parameters of what it is I should be looking at. And I should add that, even though I was involved, certainly my opinions were taken into consideration I'm sure at any points in the investigations and also for preparation for trial. I don't have any particular personal stake in the outcome of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, sir, that your position is actually very different from that of an academic expert, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I know the Tribunal treats internal experts differently from external experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you some other questions. You told us -- you were born in the United States. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in St. Paul, Minnesota.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of any other country?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you hold a passport from any other country?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have the United Nations LP for travel, but, no, I have no other citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And what's the ethnic origin of your family, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're probably more interested in my father's family. My mother's family is partly -- mainly German, partly English. My mother has no connection with the former Yugoslavia other than marrying my father. And my grandparents, the last time they came to the United States was shortly before my father's birth. So it -- they probably would have come to the United States about 1925, give or take a year, my grandparents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I'm not sure you answered the question, but your ethnic origin is --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On your father's side.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. And do I gather, then, from what you said that your grandparents emigrated from Croatia to the United States? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give or take a year. Certainly before 1927, because my father was born in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And did you learn Croatian, grow up speaking it at home, or did --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit, because my grandmother never did learn to speak English particularly well. So I learned some at home. And then I learned more travelling to Zagreb while I was in university, and I studied it in university. And then I became really proficient using it as an historian, both as an undergraduate and as a graduate student.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, of course, at the ICTY we're generally supposed to refer to the language as B/C/S. What do you call it when you're not here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, if I was talking to a Bosnian friend -- it depends. What I would be speaking I would call Croatian. If they're a Bosnian friend or a Serbian friend I would call what they're speaking Croatian or Serbian. And then I know quite frequently in the United States, amongst mixed groups of people, we just frequently call it "nas jezik", or "our language" generically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Did your grandparents emigrate for political reasons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Purely for very, very pressing economic reasons. My grandfather had to come three times. He could never find work going home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient moment to take a break? I think I've lost track of time a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 25 to 6.00. We will have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume in 20 minutes exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to know whether I'm going too fast for the French booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, I'm told by the legal officer that you would like to clarify an answer that you gave previously; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy. I just realised when I sat down here, looking at the transcript, that I misspoke. I didn't want to give the impression that I would call what somebody Bosnian speaks Croatian. If I was talking to someone who was Bosnian or Serbian, I should say that I would call what they were speaking Bosnian or Serbian, and what I would be speaking, Croatian. I didn't mean to imply that Bosnians are speaking Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. As an historian with a particular interest in the Balkans, I would imagine you take an active interest in Croatian politics?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although certainly much more now than before I started working here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, of course, with your ethnic origin, that would also give you an interest in what happens in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If you can't answer this question, or you'd like me to put it in a different way, please tell me: As between the politics of the Tudjman administration and the president -- present government of Croatia, where does your preference lie?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my preference both before and after working here, and it doesn't influence my work, but my preference would definitely be politically with the current president, Mr. Mesic, rather than Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you would disapprove of some of the actions or decisions taken by the Tudjman administration?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be hard to -- to work here and see everything I've seen and not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the period round about 1990, 1991. Were you at that time following events in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Both as an historian, or at least an advanced student of history, and also someone who had a personal interest in what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a very direct interest. I was supposed to have gone to Zagreb in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did it become apparent to you at some particular time that the former Yugoslavia was on the point of dissolution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I think I can just about date -- I always have one particular memory in mind of that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that date was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember being in the -- I think it was in the basement of the Yale library, and this would have been late 1988, early 1989, and reading a copy of Nin, which is a Serbian news weekly and thinking to myself, Good heavens, if what's -- if they -- if whoever wrote this believes what they wrote, war is a real possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia began, as we know, certain of the -- of what had previously been republics within the federation began to become independent states, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: First of all Slovenia and then Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And after that, the question arose of what would happen to Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: At that time, what was your opinion as to what the political solution in Bosnia and Herzegovina should be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Apologies to Mr. Murphy for interrupting. Your Honour, I've been silent up until now, but I think some of these things, we're getting far afield from what is really relevant to this testimony. The witness has indicated a number of times already that his personal opinions did not enter into his work. I've certainly allowed Mr. Murphy to go on for some considerable period as to his personal feelings and background, but I think now we're getting into things that -- unless there's some showing -- there can be some showing of some connection, I think we should move forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has presented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, what is the relevance? What is the link? Because I can see that you're asking him about his political opinions. You could have quite easily said that they're manifested in a vote. He's played along with you. He's answered your questions. You're following the same line of questioning, though, which means that there is something you want to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The witness has presented himself as being a neutral and objective expert, and it was simply my intention to explore the extent of his neutrality, so to speak. But I can do that quite briefly and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let me just pose one specific question, then, sir, and I'll move on. Was it your opinion that Bosnia and Herzegovina should become an independent state with a heterogeneous population?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't see any real viable alternative to that. Certainly the borders which were established, the so-called AVNOJ borders or the post World War II borders between the republics certainly might not be ideal, and certainly you leave a lot of people on the wrong side of a frontier if you draw lines. But I'm not sure they could be improved upon necessarily, and plus that -- that opens up all sorts of other problems if you start interfering with those borders. Certainly, personally, the solution I would have liked to have seen most is any solution which would have allowed people in Bosnia and Herzegovina to be able to live where they did before the war and continue to live there and continue to live normal lives as they did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to move on to ask you some questions about the HZ HB and the HR HB, as you have given evidence about them. First of all, I think we're agreed that the decision on taking the -- on founding the HZ HB was taken on the 18th of November, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formal decision, yes, although the decision to make that decision was made on the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at that time, this was some time before Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by the United States and the European Union; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you remember when that recognition was given to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's the first week of April, I think, and I'm not positive, April 6th, of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. So when the HZ HB was established, it was established on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina but before that territory was recognised as an independent state. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if you would now, sir, turn -- I have a number of questions to ask you based on your report, if you have that available, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if the members of the Court have the report, I'm going to page 10 initially, and paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you're dealing there with a particular document. Can you remind us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's citation number 20, those would be the conclusions of the meeting of the 12th of November, 1991, which is the meeting I was discussing just a second ago, which is the decision to decide to establish Herceg-Bosna in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look down in paragraph 13, about seven lines from the bottom, there is a phrase quoted from the document, "... forces in favour of a non-existent sovereign BiH," and at the time that phrase was quite accurate, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're thinking in terms of international recognition, yes. However, my reading of that is that they're referring to persons like Mr. Kljuic, who were still in favour of Bosnian -- Bosnian integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Then the citation goes on, "... in which the Croatian people would be condemned to genocide and elimination from history." Now, would you agree, based on your research, that that kind of language of mutual accusations -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Let me start again. When you referred to that -- actually, to that citation by the witness, that is, with all these forces, "that we tried to stop these inevitable forces," et cetera, there you referred to the transcript but I did not find it, "...in which the Croatian people would be condemned to genocide and elimination from history." I frankly don't find that one. Is it in the same paragraph 13 or do you take that -- that part of your quotation from another document -- I mean from another place in this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, it's in paragraph 13 of the report, Your Honour, on page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I see now that in that -- because, frankly, I merely studied the paragraph 13 and the footnote 20, and afterwards 22, but now I see that you quoted that particular part after footnote 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: "... party leadership at that time that there were still forces in favour of a non-existent," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Now I found it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, language of that kind, in your experience, talking about genocide and elimination, was used by all parties to the conflict at different times, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Individuals from all parties used language like that in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: As a form, in a way, of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although in some instances fairly well justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It's not unusual for states or entities who feel threatened to -- to use propaganda of that kind, is it? Well, let me give you a concrete example. You're familiar with the phrase "the axis of evil," aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Isn't it a fairly normal reaction of a state that perceives itself to be under threat to use strong language about their perceived enemy; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes, although I don't think in the case of the axis of evil that particular inflammatory language was justified. But sometimes people -- sometimes politicians do use inflammatory language, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's really, I think, my point. At the time when the HZ HB was established, it was a time of great uncertainty in the former Yugoslavia. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. At the same time it was established, the city of Vukovar fell to the JNA and Serb forces, and there was a pitched war going on in Croatia. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, indeed, to some extent at least, the JNA and the Serb forces were using the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from which to launch an attack against Croatia. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, as you point out in your report, shortly before the HZ HB was established, the Serbs had set up their own entities, the beginning to -- what eventually became the so-called Serb autonomous areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it wouldn't be an exaggeration to say that at that time the Serbs represented a serious military threat to the non-Serb inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
